claim: No conclusive evidence that difficult general knowledge questions cause a 'Google Stroop effect'.
counterexample: This is the verbatim title of a published, peer-reviewed replication study: Hesselmann, G. (2020). 'No conclusive evidence that difficult general knowledge questions cause a "Google Stroop effect". A replication study.' PeerJ 8:e10325. The claim as written is not an original assertion — it is the title of an existing paper. If the piece presents this phrase as its own conclusion or as an unattributed finding, it is reproducing the title of Hesselmann (2020) without attribution. If the piece cites Hesselmann (2020) correctly, the sentence is fine. The 'break' is that the phrase is not the piece's own finding: it already exists as a published paper title.
quote: "No conclusive evidence that difficult general knowledge questions cause a 'Google Stroop effect'. A replication study"
why_it_still_matters: If the piece presents this as its own conclusion without citing Hesselmann (2020), it is an attribution error. If it cites Hesselmann correctly, the sentence survives. The underlying finding — that the Google Stroop effect did not replicate — is real and published. The break is sourcing, not substance.
inherited_from: Hesselmann, G. (2020). PeerJ 8:e10325. The original Sparrow, Liu & Wegner (2011) Science paper claimed the effect; Hesselmann (2020) is the registered replication that failed to confirm it.
